title: S-corp election analysis
summary: Above ~$50–80K net profit, electing S-corp status can save thousands annually in self-employment tax — but adds payroll complexity.
detailsHtml:
The mechanics

An LLC or partnership can elect to be taxed as an S-corp by filing Form 2553. The owner-employee then takes a "reasonable salary" (subject to payroll tax) plus "distributions" (not subject to payroll tax). Self-employment tax of 15.3% applies only to the salary portion, not the distributions — saving 15.3% × (net profit − reasonable salary).

Comparison at $150K net business income: Sole proprietor: SE tax: $150K × 92.35% × 15.3% = ~$21,200 S-corp with $70K reasonable salary: Payroll tax on salary: $70K × 15.3% = $10,710 Distributions: $80K, no SE tax SE tax savings: ~$10,500 Less: payroll service costs (~$1,000/year) Less: tax prep complexity (~$500-1,500/year) Net annual savings: ~$8,000-9,000
The "reasonable salary" trap — IRS enforcement posture has hardened. The IRS uses a comparable-wage methodology (RC Reports, BLS OEWS, ERI compensation data) rather than a percentage rule; the burden of proof is on the taxpayer to document. Recent Tax Court memoranda (Maggard v. Comm'r, T.C. Memo 2024-77; the Sean McAlary Ltd. line; Glass Blocks Unlimited) reinforce that distributions can be recharacterized as wages when salary is unreasonably low for the role. The $1 salary referenced in older planning literature as "fraudulent" is the extreme; the actual audit-risk zone for personal-service businesses (consulting, professional services, agency owners) begins at salary ratios under ~40% of net business income. The $70K-on-$150K example above (47%) is reasonable for many businesses but is on the lower end for pure-service businesses where the owner is the principal revenue generator. Many tax attorneys advise professional-services owners to target 60–70% salary ratios to remove the issue from audit consideration — accepting ~$3–5K of additional payroll tax annually in exchange for examination immunity is a defensible trade most planners recommend at $300K+ net income. Document with comparable-wage data (RC Reports, BLS OEWS) in the working papers.

When NOT to elect S-corp

Below ~$50K net profit, the payroll costs and complexity eat the savings. With wildly variable income (some years high, some near zero), the rigidity of S-corp salary requirements creates problems. With plans to scale to multiple employees, an LLC or C-corp may serve better long-term.
